<section class="proj-q" aria-labelledby="h-question">
<h2 id="h-question"><i class="bi bi-question-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Research question</h2>
<p class="proj-question">Can existing and new U.S. nuclear power plants improve their economics and operating flexibility by adding high-temperature electrolysis, hydrogen storage and batteries, and by selling energy, hydrogen and ancillary services?</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-insight" id="insight" aria-labelledby="h-insight">
<h2 id="h-insight"><i class="bi bi-stars" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key insight</h2>
<p class="insight-title">With the assumed hydrogen credit, hydrogen revenue can sustain an existing reactor but not pay for a new one</p>
<p>The study treats an existing reactor&#x27;s capital as already spent, so revenue from power, hydrogen and reserves, with the assumed hydrogen credit, must cover running costs and the new equipment; most reactors studied then reached positive net present value. A new plant must also recover the reactor&#x27;s capital cost, and new builds stayed below zero even with tax credits.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec proj-explainer" id="explainer" aria-labelledby="h-explainer">
<h2 id="h-explainer"><i class="bi bi-sliders" aria-hidden="true"></i>Why does hydrogen help an existing reactor more than a new one?</h2>
<div class="explainer" data-explainer="npph2">
<p class="ex-fallback">A reactor earns from electricity; with an electrolyzer it can also sell hydrogen and offer reserves, and a hydrogen production credit adds to that. The study treats an existing reactor&#x27;s capital as already spent, so these revenues need to cover operating costs and the new equipment. A new plant must also recover the reactor&#x27;s capital cost, and in the study the same revenues did not cover it.</p>
</div>
<p class="ex-note"><i class="bi bi-info-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study&#x27;s data or results.</p>
</section>
<script src="../assets/explainers/common.js" defer></script>
<script src="../assets/explainers/npph2.js" defer></script>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-contribution">
<h2 id="h-contribution"><i class="bi bi-person-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>My contribution</h2>
<p>First author. I did most of the work: the methodology, the optimization and lifetime techno-economic models (developed during my internship at Idaho National Laboratory), the analysis and the writing.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" id="approach" aria-labelledby="h-approach">
<h2 id="h-approach"><i class="bi bi-tools" aria-hidden="true"></i>How I approached it</h2>
<ol class="approach">
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>Seven U.S. markets price energy and ancillary services differently, and each of 42 reactors faces its own prices.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I co-developed an hourly dispatch model that co-optimizes electricity sales, hydrogen production, storage and ancillary services under each market&#x27;s products, run for every reactor.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>It showed how market design, not only the reactor, shapes the value of flexibility.</p></li>
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>Electrolyzers and turbines are not ideal: efficiency varies with load, starts wear equipment, and ramping is limited.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I helped represent turbine and electrolyzer efficiency with piecewise-linear curves, track electrolyzer degradation from operation and start-ups, and enforce ramp limits and minimum stable load.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>Flexibility estimates then respect what the equipment can actually do.</p></li>
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>One year of hourly dispatch had to become a lifetime investment case under several federal credits.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I co-developed a discounted cash-flow model with component-level capital costs, scheduled replacements and the 45U, 45V-type, 45Y and 48E credits, linked to the dispatch results.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>The same operation could be judged as a retrofit (with and without 45U) or as a new build (no credit, 45Y or 48E); the hydrogen credit is assumed throughout.</p></li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" id="choices" aria-labelledby="h-choices">
<h2 id="h-choices"><i class="bi bi-signpost-split" aria-hidden="true"></i>Design choices</h2>
<dl class="choices">
<div class="choice"><dt>Take electricity and hydrogen prices as given (price-taking)</dt><dd><span class="ch-alt">Alternatives considered: equilibrium or game-theoretic market models with price feedback</span>The study evaluates plant operation against observed 2024 prices; price feedback from wide adoption is stated as a limit and left to future work.</dd></div>
</dl>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-method">
<h2 id="h-method"><i class="bi bi-diagram-3" aria-hidden="true"></i>Method</h2>
<p>Hourly mixed-integer optimization of turbine, electrolyzer and storage dispatch for 42 reactors in seven U.S. ISO/RTO markets using 2024 prices, linked to a lifetime cash-flow model with federal tax credits (45U, a 45V-type hydrogen credit, 45Y and 48E).</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-findings">
<h2 id="h-findings"><i class="bi bi-lightbulb" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key findings</h2>
<ol class="findings">
<li>Operated as baseload-only plants at 2024 market prices, nearly all reactors studied had negative net present value.</li>
<li>With hydrogen integration, including the assumed hydrogen production credit, a majority of the reactors reached positive net present value.</li>
<li>Integrated operation added output flexibility; ancillary-service revenue was a few percent of the total.</li>
<li>For new builds, investment and production tax credits substantially lowered the levelized cost of hydrogen.</li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec proj-bounds" aria-labelledby="h-bounds">
<h2 id="h-bounds"><i class="bi bi-exclamation-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Boundary conditions</h2>
<p>Results rely on 2024 prices, price-taking market participation, modeled ancillary-service participation parameters, the assumed hydrogen credit ($3/kg for ten years) and a dispatch held fixed after the credit expires; price feedback from large-scale adoption is not modeled.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-next" id="led-to" aria-labelledby="h-next">
<h2 id="h-next"><i class="bi bi-arrow-right-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>What it led to</h2>
<p>New plants did not pay for themselves here, which raised the question of what could cover a new reactor&#x27;s capital cost; AI data centers are the candidate buyer my next studies examine. <a class="next-link" href="nuclear-dc.html">Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center<i class="bi bi-arrow-right" aria-hidden="true"></i></a></p>
</section>
